v.why: At very large learning rates wider layers amplify the effective function-space step and push training further past the divergence cliff.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise that otherwise destabilises training at high learning rates.
Deeper nets have a sharper stability cliff so a one-step learning-rate increase more often causes divergence.
Large batches give few updates per epoch, so a larger learning rate compensates and reduces undertraining.
Very wide nets already have ample capacity, so extra depth mostly adds optimization difficulty and overfitting.
With tiny learning rates, more layers give more parameters moving per Adam step and so faster effective progress.
With few updates from large batches, wider nets fit faster per step and so reduce undertraining.
Deeper nets amplify the noise of tiny-batch gradients, making training less stable.
A single hidden layer gets its capacity only from width, so widening helps more than when depth already supplies capacity.
Narrow nets have little spare capacity, so stronger L2 shrinkage pushes them into underfitting.
